Ok, I switched to embedded "routers" as late and 2005'ish and haven't looked back. In fact, I don't even have an ATX PC anymore, Cubieboards, Raspberry Pi's and such are so much less hassle for specific-purpose computing and high-end laptops are nowadays all I needed from a desktop setup, but frees me from chairs and desks.

I wanted a robust firewall + router solution and my Netgear w/ DD-WRT just wasn't doing it, and I had spare components laying around so I went with it. Then I just liked how PfSense had a better GUI and more ways I can customize whenever I wanted it. I just felt like I had more power over my own network.

There is a ton of stuff people can learn with something like pfSense that you can't really get out of a stock consumer router. I'm not trying to sell it as a perfect device for everyone, but if someone is already well-versed in networking or would like to learn more, it's a powerhouse in terms of cost:capability. Even for the not-so-technologically inclined, it's very user-friendly. For instance, it's a nice way to run Snort IDS, or a perimeter firewall with SPI, or host an OpenVPN server if you'd like to VPN back to your home connection while you are away or set-up a site-to-site tunnel for friends who would like to securely share content. It combines a ton of resources and capability into one well-supported box, and gives a person tons of fine-grained control over their network connections.

As for power consumption, yes it consumes power, but the Core2 and newer Intel processors really don't use as much as people might think. For instance, Core2Duo chips get around 4.2x better performance per watt ratio than P4s.

http://www.tomshardware.com/reviews/intel-cpu-power-consumption,1750.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_CPU_power_dissipation_figures

Depending on the hardware, you can also put pfSense (or other software firewall appliance) on a hypervisor. VMware ESXi with hardware passthru (like Direct I/O) to a dual-port PCI-E NIC is a great option. Then you can run your security appliance while using the tower to host (an)other virtual server(s), like FreePBX, LAMP/FTP/Plex server, or whatever you might need/want to play with like a secondary pfSense or other firewall install used for testing. If you're going to keep a PC plugged in and up 24x7, you might as well get some use out of the hardware!

Note: The linked website wasn't opening for me, so I haven't been able to read the article. If this was mentioned in it, I apologize and please let me know.

Edit: There are reasonable concerns about placing a security appliance on top of a virtualized sublayer. Without getting too crazy about it, if you properly set-up and secure access to your hypervisor, these issues really shouldn't matter too much for the average user.

Well, for one, it doesn't interact with electromagnetic sources, which includes light. This means that you can't "see" dark matter because it neither reflects or absorbs light. It also makes up about 27% of our universe, while normal matter (things you can touch and see) makes up only 5%. The reason we believe dark matter exists is because the amount of matter in galaxies isn't enough to have them form from gravity or even keep them together. So there must be other "stuff" there that we haven't detected yet. We don't know how to describe it, or even what it does other than it is affected by gravity, so we call it dark matter.
